person.note: He was the son of Tippādhvarin, one of the recipients of the land donation at Thiruvisanallur, and so was a native of Thiruvisanallur. See A Descriptive Catalogue of the Sanskrit Manuscripts in the Sarasvati Mahal Library, Tanjore (Tanjore). Vols. 1–19: Vol. 8, p. 3371.

He was the younger contemporary of Cokkanāthamakhin, hence the name of this entry (Cokkanāthamakhin younger), and belonged to the early 18th century. See A Descriptive Catalogue of the Sanskrit Manuscripts in the Sarasvati Mahal Library, Tanjore (Tanjore). Vols. 1–19: vol. 8, p. xxxi–xxxii.

He was active roughly two decades after the inauguration of Thiruvisanallur. (See Ariav, Talia, Intimately Cosmopolitan: Genealogical Poets and Orchestrated Selves in 17–18th Century Sanskrit Literature from South India, 2022: p. 32).

He resided in Thiruvisanallur before traveling to Karnataka. (See Ariav, Talia, Intimately Cosmopolitan: Genealogical Poets and Orchestrated Selves in 17–18th Century Sanskrit Literature from South India, 2022: p. 32, n. 77)

He was the last of five brothers (Kuppādhvarin, Tirumalādhvarin, Svāmi Śāstrin, Sītārāma Śāstrin, and Cokkanātha). Alongside his rather, his brother Kuppādhvarin was also a recipient of the land donation at Thiruvisanallur. (See Raghavan, Venkataraman. Śāhendravilāsa of Śrīdhara Veṅkaṭeśa (A Poem on the Life of King Śāhaji of Tanjore, 1684-1710). Tiruchi: The Kalyan Press, 1952: p. 56).

He was patronised directly by King Śāhaji. (See Raghavan, Venkataraman. Śāhendravilāsa of Śrīdhara Veṅkaṭeśa (A Poem on the Life of King Śāhaji of Tanjore, 1684-1710). Tiruchi: The Kalyan Press, 1952: p. 55).

He was the last of five brothers (Kuppādhvarin, Tirumalādhvarin, Svāmi Śāstrin, Sītārāma Śāstrin, and Cokkanātha). Alongside his father, his brother Kuppādhvarin was also a recipient of the land donation at Thiruvisanallur. (See Raghavan, Venkataraman. Śāhendravilāsa of Śrīdhara Veṅkaṭeśa (A Poem on the Life of King Śāhaji of Tanjore, 1684-1710). Tiruchi: The Kalyan Press, 1952: p. 56).

Later, he was patronised by Basava, likely Ikkeri Basava Nāyaka (1691–1714). (See Raghavan, Venkataraman. Kunjunni (1946). ‘The Bālavyutpattikāriṇī of Śokkanātha. In The Adyar Library Bulletin 10(4): p. 115).
